In the U.S. alone, farmers use about 280 million pounds of glyphosate every year. The general public also uses glyphosate to kill weeds on their lawns. Glyphosate is also used heavily on schoolyards, forests and even rangelands. So itÂ is hardly surprising that glyphosate has apparently been harming wildlife and habitats.

The EPA has asked the public for comments after releasing their findings. Officials plan to consult with federal agencies toÂ determine how best to protect endangered plants and animals from glyphosate exposure.

Unfortunately, the EPA has had a wishy-washy approach to regulating the use of glyphosate with regards to its reported adverse effects on human health. InÂ its report, the agencyÂ said glyphosate is not likely carcinogenic to humans.

However, theÂ International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC)Â determinedÂ that glyphosate was a probable human carcinogen in 2015. The EPA had even agreed with this classification before it backtracked. Last October, itapproved the use of Bayer AG’s glyphosate-based weedkiller Roundupfor the next five years.

Given the EPA’s inconsistencies regarding its verdict on glyphosate, the advocacyÂ group Center for Food Safety (CFS)filed a lawsuit against the agencylast March in the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals. Representing a broad coalition of farmers and conservationists, the CFS seeksÂ to have glyphosate prohibited from use or sale to protect users from its adverse effects.

Last December, the CFS filed its opening arguments and evidence in its litigation challenging the EPA’s approval of the controversial herbicide. (Related:ÂMexico bans GM corn, plans to phase out imports and the use of Monsantoâs glyphosate.)

But that is not the first time that glyphosateÂ became the subject of a lawsuit. When the German pharmaceutics company Bayer AG acquired the agrochemical company Monsanto in 2018, it also acquiredÂ thousands of lawsuits against Monsanto from farmers and customers that allegedÂ Roundup gave themcancer.

Christine Sheppard, one of over 800 cancer patients who sued Monsanto,Â saidshe used Roundup toÂ eliminate weeds in her coffee farm in Hawaii before falling illin 2003. Physicians later found several enlarged lymph nodes inside her. She was diagnosed withÂ stage 4 non-Hodgkin’slymphomaand was forced to stop farm work.

Former school groundskeeperDewayne JohnsonÂ also suedÂ MonsantoÂ after he was diagnosed with the same disease. He used Roundup to maintain school grounds and sports fields. In 2018, a judge ordered that Monsanto pay Johnson $289 million after a jury ruled thatÂ glyphosate caused Johnson’s cancer.
